new_statements.quote: Stress in Yale seems to be primarily sonority-driven. The basic stress assignment algorithm seems to be something like the following. (19) 1. Mark the last syllable as extrametrical. 2. Assign primary stress to a penultimate /a/. 3. If there is none, assign stress to an antipenultimate /a/. 4. If there is none, run the above two steps with /ɛ/ instead. 5. Make the primary stressed syllable the head of a foot, and make feet around it as space allows. Feet can be iambic or trochaic; the choice is determined by which allows the maximum number of footed syllables. [...] However, the majority of Yale words seem to have no noticeable stress at all.
new_statements.citation: Aannestad, Aidan, Carl Campbell & Jody Campbell. 2020. Towards a grammar of the Yale language: taking another look at archived field data. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG, unpublished manuscript (dated 25 September 2020), 105 pp.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The language is (tentatively) tonal — 'It seems clear that tone is phonemic' (p. 21) — and 'stress is dependent on tone (and vowel quality)' (p. 20). Word stress, where present, is sonority-driven inside a right-edge three-syllable window: the final syllable is extrametrical; primary stress goes to a penultimate /a/, failing that an antepenultimate /a/, failing that a penultimate then antepenultimate /ɛ/. If no non-final /a/ or /ɛ/ exists the word has no stress; all monosyllables and disyllables are stressless (a degenerate foot is disallowed), as are words whose pitch pattern clashes with stress (falling pitch on a weak syllable, stress on the second of two high syllables, all-low words incl. most loans). Words with a penultimate falling pitch are stressed on that syllable regardless of vowel. Vowel reduction in metrically weak syllables is the diagnostic for stress. Examples: agoˈsaba 'grass', ˈakola 'fire pit', faˈlakɛ 'single man', leˈglɛsi 'wall'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Feet are built around the primary-stressed syllable, iambic or trochaic as needed to foot the most syllables; secondary stress on the non-adjacent foot head, e.g. walugaluju 'mouth harp' -> (ˌwalu)(ˈgalu)ju (p. 23); tobali-afɛ 'five times' [to²ˈba⁴li¹ˌa¹fɛ¹] (p. 24).
new_statements.exceptions: Majority of words stressless (all mono- and disyllables; words lacking non-final /a/ or /ɛ/, e.g. hoklifa 'ant', tetekei 'sweet potato'; words with disallowed stress-tone combinations; all-low-pitch words incl. most Tok Pisin/English loans). Words with penultimate falling pitch are stressed there irrespective of vowel (ɛˈniːno 'tooth', aˈmeːgi 'tongs'); compounds and multimorphemic words 'complex and unpredictable' (p. 24). Author flags open questions: stress-tone combinations, compound stress, stress in inflected verbs/auxiliaries (p. 25). Footnote 9: no evidence that syllable weight influences placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, based mainly on nouns elicited in the frame 'ɛbe X' ('this is an X') on 1984-2000 tape recordings; the author never did fieldwork and calls the whole prosodic analysis tentative ('seems'). Sonority-driven vowel-quality stress in a tonal language; the language of the analysis could equally be filed as weight-sensitive (vowel-quality sonority) — the 'tonal-with-stress-statement' reading is chosen because the source itself makes tone primary and stress dependent on it.
new_statements.first_reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes the Yale language proper (Yadë/Yalë, formerly 'Nagatman'; ISO nce, glottocode yale1246) of the Yale villages, Sandaun Province, PNG; no dialects are distinguished. Data are the Campbells' 1984-2015 archived recordings and notes, reanalysed by Aannestad without fieldwork, so the prosodic description is explicitly tentative.
